so wait — is the whole label just wrong then? i need to know before i talk to mary alice.

The object can still be real. The **label, as written, is not defensible.**

That sentence makes four claims. Even if Mary Alice’s 1882 account book is exactly what she says it is, it only really backs **one** of them:

| Claim on the wall | What the ledger (as described) actually supports |
|---|---|
| There was a pattern draft in **1882** | Yes — commission date |
| **Novice Maria Soran** did the initial design | Yes — one named novice, a draft |
| Created by **convent novices** (plural) | No — that’s one person, not a novice workshop |
| Created **exclusively** by them | No — “exclusive” is not in the source |
| This **is** the St. Jude lace pattern / tradition | No — a commissioned draft ≠ a named, exclusive convent tradition |

So: not “the whole story is fake.” The **wording** is wrong. “Exclusively by convent novices in 1882” is the part that will not survive a careful reader, a donor, or another historian.

Before you talk to Mary Alice, go in with this:

- Thank her for the ledger. Keep 1882 and Soran if the book really says that.
- Drop **exclusively**.
- Don’t turn one novice’s draft into a convent-wide origin myth.
- Put the credit on the wall the way the source puts it.

Safer line:

> Pattern draft commissioned in 1882; initial design credited to novice Maria Soran (diocesan workshop account book).

That’s the version that holds up. The current one doesn’t.
